q-north.name: Diani North — the river end
q-north.teaser: Where the strip runs out into estuary, baobab and a coral mosque that has outlived every hotel
q-north.story: Diani began at its northern end, where the Mwachema river, locally the Kongo, slides out of the mangroves into the sea. Giant baobabs stand over the mouth, and among them a working coral mosque, its history kept for the culture pages. South of it, around Colliers Centre, the addresses turn Italian, and the hotel sand in front of them is the quietest on the strip. This end keeps its own evening timetable: the dugout canoes push off up the river at sunset, and at low tide people wade the mouth across to Tiwi. Sit here once with a green coconut and the middle of Diani feels loud.
q-north.why: Come late on a falling tide: estuary, baobabs and the evening boats all share one stretch of sand.
facts: Gombato side, north of Colliers Centre, at the Mwachema mouth
The baobabs over the estuary and the coral mosque among them
The sunset dugout up the river, told under the boats

q-central.name: Diani Central
q-central.teaser: Hotels, bars and dive shops back to back behind the whitest sand, and a week here needs no car
q-central.story: This is the Diani of the postcards and also the part that keeps the whole strip running. Behind the whitest stretch of sand, hotels, bars and dive shops stand shoulder to shoulder; around them sit the supermarkets, the beach clubs, the tourist police post and Ali Barbour's, the restaurant built down inside a coral cave. Everything is walkable and nothing is far, which is the whole case for staying here. If you have one week and no car, take a room on this stretch and you will never miss having one. The trade-off is company: the most convenient sand on the coast is also the most used.
q-central.why: Stay here if you are not driving: food, dive desks and groceries are all a short walk apart.
facts: Between the Ukunda junction turnoff and Nomad
On foot along the beach or the road from anywhere mid-strip
Supermarkets, dive shops and the tourist police post
Ali Barbour's Cave Restaurant, booked ahead

q-galu.name: Galu & the southern strip
q-galu.teaser: The beach changes its name south of Nomad, and the pace of the day drops by half
q-galu.story: South of Nomad the sand takes another name, Galu, in Kinondo ward, and the strip settles into its mellower second act. There are fewer walls along the beach, and the reef flat in front of it is wider at low tide, which is why the kite schools treat this as home water. Fishermen land their catch at Mwaepe, the landing you can walk to from the Galu hotels, and Pallet Cafe, the deaf-staffed cafe, serves on the sand. On the way down the canopy closes over the road and monkeys cross on rope above the traffic; the green section tells that story.
q-galu.why: Base yourself here for space and wind: the kite water and the fish landing are both on the doorstep.
facts: South of Nomad down to Kinondo Kwetu country
The kite schools' launch sand and the Mwaepe fish landing
The wide reef flat at spring low, told under walks

q-ukunda.name: Ukunda town
q-ukunda.teaser: Twenty minutes from the sunbeds: matatus, banks, markets, the airstrip, and the food locals actually eat
q-ukunda.story: Ukunda is the actual town, a workaday Swahili-Digo service centre on the A14 highway, where the people who keep Diani running live, bank and shop. The matatus start here, the banks are here, and the airstrip lies just off the strip road. So is the real food: mahamri fried at dawn by the women at their stalls, grills at the junction once the light goes, biryani rooms at lunch. The new covered market and the cheapest supermarket in the area are both here as well. It is twenty minutes from the sunbeds and a different world, and it is the half of the coast that most visitors never see.
q-ukunda.why: Eat in Ukunda at least once: breakfast mahamri or a junction grill tells you more than any hotel menu.
facts: Inland, at the A14 junction; the airstrip is on the strip road
The new covered market at Mvindeni and the biryani rooms
Mahamri at dawn; the junction grills after dark
The morning town walk, under walks

q-tiwi.name: Tiwi
q-tiwi.teaser: Wade the river mouth on the ebb and the beach on the far side is nearly empty
q-tiwi.story: Across the Mwachema river lies Tiwi, Diani's quieter cousin: low-key cottages, a campsite and essentially no restaurant scene. Villas cater for themselves and fishermen sell their catch directly on the sand. Twiga Lodge is the one kitchen anyone has documented, and recent reports on it are mixed, so check that it is running before you count on lunch. The best way in is on foot. At low tide you wade the river mouth from the Kongo Mosque and step onto sand with hardly anyone on it; come back before the flood. By car it is the long way round via the highway, on rough access roads.
q-tiwi.why: Walk over on a falling tide for near-empty sand, and keep the access roads for daylight only.
facts: Wade from the Kongo Mosque at low tide, or drive round via the highway
Fishermen selling their catch on the sand
Twiga Lodge, if its kitchen is running
The walk back before the tide floods the mouth

q-likoni.name: Likoni & Dongo Kundu — the arrival
q-likoni.teaser: The old ferry or the new bypass: since August 2024 the south coast finally has a choice of front door
q-likoni.story: For decades the south coast began in a queue at the Likoni ferry, which at its peak carried more than 300,000 people a day across the harbour mouth. In August 2024 the Dongo Kundu bypass opened to the public, carried over the water on the bridge described among the landmarks, and Diani became a clean drive from Mombasa's airport. Now there is a real choice: the ferry for the crowded, very Mombasa crossing, the bypass for a quick transfer. No toll was charged at the last dated report, but the Treasury approved a tolling plan in September 2025, so check before you set out. Arrival logistics are in the appendix.
q-likoni.why: Take the bypass for the transfer, and the ferry once, on foot, to see how the coast used to start.
facts: Mombasa's south side, between the island and the Kwale coast
Likoni ferry from Mombasa island, or the Dongo Kundu bypass from the airport side
A toll on the bypass: none at last report, but one is planned

sources.label: The Standard: Treasury gives green light to Dongo Kundu tolling plan

q-kinondo.name: Kinondo & Chale point
q-kinondo.teaser: Rural Digo country behind the last of the sand, where the forest is a shrine
q-kinondo.story: Behind the southern end of Galu the beach gives way to rural Digo country, and the land itself is the reason to come. Here is Kaya Kinondo, the one sacred forest open to visitors, along with the quietest lodges on the coast and the health centre that the Swedish family behind Kinondo Kwetu built for the village. The kaya's visiting rules work as the etiquette of the whole area: this is somebody's parish, so dress and behave accordingly. Further south the mainland ends at Chale point, about 10 km below the strip, facing a forested island 600 metres out whose resort has its own card.
q-kinondo.why: Come for the kaya walk and stay for the quiet: nothing on this coast feels further from the resort strip.
facts: Behind Galu's southern end, down to Chale point
The kaya forest, the small lodges and the village health centre
Kinondo Kwetu, by prior arrangement only
Kaya Kinondo, walked with a Digo guide

q-gazi-msambweni.name: Gazi & Msambweni
q-gazi-msambweni.teaser: A mangrove village the scientists know by name, then kilometres of sand with nobody on it
q-gazi-msambweni.story: Two places south of the resort zone, and both are working towns rather than stops. Gazi, about 25 km down the A14, is a fishing village on a mangrove bay whose community carbon project is now copied worldwide; the green section tells it. Eat where the villagers eat and pay your guide properly. Further on lies Msambweni, the sub-county town, with a fishing economy, administrative offices and kilometres of beach with nobody on them. Go for that emptiness, with your own water and your own arrangements, and expect no services at all.
q-gazi-msambweni.why: Pair them in one morning: the Gazi mangroves on the tide, then Msambweni's empty sand.
facts: Gazi about 25 km south off the A14; Msambweni about 45 min south of the strip
The mangrove edge at Gazi; empty beach at Msambweni

q-shimoni-wasini.name: Shimoni & Wasini
q-shimoni-wasini.teaser: A dhow harbour heavy with history, and across the channel an island with no roads and no cars
q-shimoni-wasini.story: At the far south of the Kenyan coast, about 75 minutes from Diani, Shimoni is a working dhow harbour and the gateway to the marine park. The Imperial British East Africa Company kept its headquarters here in the 1880s, and the coral caves by the jetty, explained under culture, held people for the slave markets. Across a 3 km channel lies Wasini, an island without a single car: a few thousand people in fishing villages, wheelbarrows on coral lanes, and an old Wa-vumba settlement built among its own ruins. Electricity reached the island only in 2023, through a solar mini-grid. The crossing itself belongs to the dhow day.
q-shimoni-wasini.why: Give Shimoni an hour on foot before the boat: the harbour makes the rest of the day make sense.
facts: Shimoni about 75 min south of Diani; Wasini 3 km across the channel
By road to Shimoni, then by boat to the island
Wheelbarrows, the only traffic on Wasini's lanes
The pillar tomb on Wasini, told in culture

sources.label: Kenya News Agency: Solar power supply project brings remote Kwale islands out of the dark

w-sunrise.name: Sunrise on the strip
w-sunrise.teaser: The emptiest hour of the resort day, and the fishermen are already pushing out
w-sunrise.story: Four degrees south of the equator the sun keeps office hours: it comes up around 06:15 all year round. The beach before seven belongs to three sets of people: the turtle programme's monitors on their morning patrol, the ngalawa crews pushing their outriggers into the water, and you. Walk north toward the river or south toward Galu, keeping to the upper beach, which stays walkable at any tide. The askaris posted along the hotel frontages are your chain of landmarks, and usually good for a greeting. It is the emptiest hour of the resort day and, for most people who try it once, the best.
w-sunrise.why: Set one alarm for 06:00: the sand, the light and the boats are never this good again later in the day.
facts: Your hotel's stretch of beach, anywhere on the strip
Your choice: north to the river or south to Galu
Upper beach sand, walkable at any tide

w-river-mouth.name: Kongo Mosque & the river mouth
w-river-mouth.teaser: Baobabs, an estuary you can wade at low water, and a coral mosque still in daily use
w-river-mouth.story: At the north end of the strip the Mwachema, called the Kongo here, meets the sea under giant baobabs. Time the walk to the ebb: at low tide the mouth is shallow enough to wade, and Tiwi's sand is on the far side. Beside the estuary stands the coral-rag Kongo Mosque, one of a tiny handful of ancient coral mosques still in use in Kenya; its history is told in the culture section. Its custodians keep rules on the neighbouring sand: dress properly, no bottles, quiet at prayer times. The madafu sellers by the mosque are the classic ones, so finish with a green coconut opened in front of you.
w-river-mouth.why: Walk it on the ebb and end with a madafu under the baobabs.
facts: Sand, plus a shallow wade across the mouth at low tide
The ebb, close to low water
A madafu from the sellers beside the mosque
Clothes that cover up for the sand by the mosque

w-reef-flat.name: The reef-flat walk
w-reef-flat.teaser: Twice a month the lagoon drains and hands you two hours of seabed, from central Diani to Galu
w-reef-flat.story: Twice a month, at the spring lows around new and full moon, the lagoon in front of Diani nearly empties and you can walk on the seabed. Between central Diani and Galu the flats are widest: seagrass, tide pools, sandbars, and water left only in the deeper channels. You share them with fishers working lines and traps, the working end of a fishery that has fed this shore for centuries. Be honest about the risks: sea urchins are plentiful, stonefish exist, and the tide comes back without consulting you. At Chale point the big lows open a smaller version facing the sacred island, where the channel fills first.
w-reef-flat.why: Start on the ebb, never the flood, and keep one eye on the water line the whole way.
facts: Central Diani, on the falling tide
Central Diani to Galu; Chale point flats as a shorter variant
Seagrass, sand and tide pools, with urchins
Spring low at new and full moon, setting out on the ebb
The fishers working their traps out on the flats
Reef shoes and the day's tide table

w-ukunda.name: Ukunda market & town walk
w-ukunda.teaser: The matatu stage, the kanga shops, the covered market and lunch at a kibanda: the strip's engine room
w-ukunda.story: Ukunda's day starts at the matatu stage, and so should the walk. From there the town opens out into its trading lanes and the new covered market at Mvindeni: produce piled on tables, tailors at their machines, spice stalls, and the smoke of mahamri that has been frying since dawn. By lunch the kibandas fill with people on their break, which is your cue to eat. Carry small notes and leave anything flashy at the hotel. If you want the doors opened, the Kaaribu street-food tour takes you through the market and into a palm-wine den, a mangwe, that an outsider would not find alone.
w-ukunda.why: Go early, before the heat and while the market is fullest, and eat where the queue is.
facts: Small notes; no valuables on show

sources.label: Kaaribu: Diani street food and market tour

w-gazi.name: Gazi Bay mangrove edge
w-gazi.teaser: The village shore of the mangrove bay every scientist in the field knows by name
w-gazi.story: Gazi is a modest fishing village about 25 km south of Diani, and its shore is among the most studied mangrove bays in the world. All nine of Kenya's mangrove species grow here, and the research station has put the village's name into journals everywhere. Walk the village edge at mid-to-high tide, when the water stands among the roots and the forest is at its fullest. This is a working place, not an attraction, so take a local guide, pay properly, and buy lunch in the village. The community carbon project that made Gazi famous is explained in the green section.
w-gazi.why: Go on a morning tide with a village guide, and stay for lunch.
facts: Gazi village shore, about 25 km south off the A14
Cash for the guide and the meal

w-shimoni.name: Shimoni history walk
w-shimoni.teaser: The caves, the 1880s company ruins, the working jetty and the channel to Wasini
w-shimoni.story: Shimoni's old dhow harbour fits into an hour or two on foot, before or after the boat crossing. Start at the working jetty, where the channel to Wasini opens in front of you and the boats load for the day. From there walk to the ruined 1880s headquarters of the IBEA Company, then go down into the coral caves with the community guide; what happened there belongs to the culture fold. It is a heavy walk and worth every minute, because it shows a quiet harbour town for what it was before the tourists came.
w-shimoni.why: Do it before the crossing if the boats allow: the caves change how you see the whole day.
facts: Village lanes; slippery coral steps in the caves
Before or after the Wasini crossing
The view down the channel to Wasini
Small cash for the cave fee

d-pilli-pipa.name: Pilli Pipa Dhow Safari
d-pilli-pipa.teaser: Marine-biologist owners, two converted jahazis, and every fee folded into one price
d-pilli-pipa.story: Pilli Pipa has run the Kisite day since 1989, and its owners are marine biologists and dive instructors, which shows in how the day is built. Hotel pickup is around 07:00, then the drive to Shimoni and a shuttle out to one of two converted jahazis, Almasi or Monsoon. An hour's sail brings you into the marine park, where you snorkel twice, one of them the sloping hard-coral wall at Inner Kisite. Lunch is at its own Wasini spot: coconut vegetable soup, crab claws, cassava bites and cardamom-clove rice. There is time for the slave caves before the drive home, back around 17:30.
d-pilli-pipa.why: Pay the all-in price and the day simply works: park fees, kit and lunch are already settled.
facts: Diani hotel pickup 07:00–07:30; the dhows sail from Shimoni
USD 137 adult / 66 child including transfers, park fees, kit and lunch; scuba add-ons USD 40–70 (seen Aug 2026)
Days ahead in season; office at Colliers Centre, daily 07:00–17:00, +254 724 442 555

d-charlie.name: Charlie Claw's dhows
d-charlie.teaser: The island restaurant's own jahazis, sailing to Kisite under a twelve-point dolphin code
d-charlie.story: The Wasini Island Restaurant, on the island since 1978, sails its own large jahazi dhows to Kisite and offers PADI and BSAC diving from them. What sets its boats apart is a published dolphin code of conduct: approach slowly and run parallel, stay no more than twenty minutes with the animals, and never swim with, feed or touch them. Its community arm pays teachers' salaries in Shimoni, Wasini and Mkwiro. There is no public tariff, so agree the whole package in writing before the day; most Diani hotels will book it for you. The crab lunch that ends the day has its own venue card.
d-charlie.why: Choose these boats if you care how the dolphins are approached: the code is written down and followed.
facts: Full day; lunch on Wasini peaks around 13:00 with the tour waves
Package on enquiry; no public tariff
+254 722 205 154, or through most Diani hotels; get it in writing

d-diy.name: Shimoni jetty, DIY
d-diy.teaser: Local captains put the same circuit together on the day for less, and you carry the checklist
d-diy.story: Local boat co-operatives at the Shimoni jetty run the same Kisite circuit, with a village lunch, for a fraction of the packaged price. The boats are mostly motorised fibreglass rather than sail, and quality varies from one to the next. Reports put locally arranged packages at around KES 3,000–4,500 a head plus park fees and a share of the boat, but nothing is published and nothing is guaranteed. The checklist is yours: agree the price, life jackets, snorkel kit, lunch and park fees before you step aboard. Be at the jetty by 08:30, ready for the tide.
d-diy.why: Settle every item before boarding, life jackets first; what you did not agree on the jetty you will not get.
facts: About KES 3,000–4,500 a head reported, plus park fees and boat share; unverified (seen Aug 2026)
On the jetty, the same morning
Cash for the boat; park fees are cashless

d-kisite.name: Kisite-Mpunguti Marine Park
d-kisite.teaser: Coral islets at the Tanzanian border where three dolphin species live all year
d-kisite.story: Gazetted in 1978, Kisite-Mpunguti covers 39 km² of coral islets off Shimoni, hard against the Tanzanian border. Three dolphin species live here: bottlenose all year on the reefs, humpback dolphins along the channel, and spinners in pods of 50 to 200. Humpback whales pass between July and October, most often in August. The water is clearest from October to March, often beyond 20 metres, and the June–August kusi chop clouds it. One honest warning: in December and January many boats reach the same reefs by mid-morning. The park is cashless and free of single-use plastic, so pack for it.
d-kisite.why: Go with the season and the tide, not against them: October to March for clear water, July to October for whales.
facts: Off Shimoni, at the Tanzanian border
Day visits; boats work the tides
Non-resident USD 25 adult / 15 child; East African KES 500; Kenya resident KES 675 (KWS schedule, Oct 2026). Good operators include it
Oct–Mar for 20 m+ visibility; Jul–Oct for whales

d-wasini-walk.name: Wasini paths & the women's boardwalk
d-wasini-walk.teaser: Coral lanes between fishing villages, then 500 metres of planks over fossil coral run by 70 women
d-wasini-walk.story: There is not one car on Wasini; the traffic on its sandy lanes and hardened coral paths is wheelbarrows. Give the hour after lunch to walking between the villages, then to the women's coral boardwalk at the village edge, a loop over fossilised coral heads and mangrove. KWS staff built it with the villagers, and the 70-member Wasini Women Group runs it; the fees go to village welfare. Come near high tide if you can, when the sea floods in beneath the dead coral and the place turns strange. The pillar tomb along the way is told in culture.
d-wasini-walk.why: Give the women the half hour and the fee: it is the gentlest part of the dhow day.
facts: Wasini village, after the lunch stop
Village lanes plus a boardwalk loop of about 500 m
Sand lanes, coral paths, weathered planks
High tide, for water under the coral
The curio shop at the boardwalk exit
Flat shoes or flip-flops; small cash, about KES 200 reported, unverified (seen Aug 2026)
d-wasini-walk.maps_query: Wasini women boardwalk coral garden Kenya

d-robinson.name: Robinson Island sandbank
d-robinson.teaser: A bar of white sand that rises at low tide and disappears again, turquoise water on every side
d-robinson.story: Off the Gazi stretch a sandbank lifts out of the sea at low tide, and the booking platforms list it, accurately, as a temporary sandbank. Glass-bottom boats run short picnic trips timed to the ebb, and the spring lows at new and full moon raise the biggest bank. There is nothing on it: white sand, turquoise all round, no shade at all. Mistime the trip and you have paid for a boat ride to open water, so check the tide time yourself rather than taking the seller's word. Pack water, and leave single-use plastic ashore: these are protected waters.
d-robinson.why: Confirm the low-water time yourself before you pay: the bank only exists for a few hours.
facts: Any beach-boat operator or hotel desk
Timed to low tide; biggest at spring lows
Glass-bottom boat trips from about USD 42 (seen Aug 2026)
Water and sun cover; no single-use plastic

d-chale.name: Chale Island
d-chale.teaser: A tidal crossing to a private-island resort, timed for a drink at Kenya's only overwater bar
d-chale.story: You reach the island only by the resort's own boat across a tidal channel from Chale point, and the hour worth timing it for is sundown at Kenya's only overwater bar. Day terms are unpublished and the island's land has been in court since 2021, so phone before you drive down.
d-chale.why: Phone first, then time the crossing so you are at the overwater bar at sundown.
facts: A sundowner at the overwater bar

sources.label: Nation: EACC recovers parcels of land in Chale Island

d-kongo-dugout.name: The Kongo River dugout
d-kongo-dugout.teaser: The sundowner that is not a bar: up the mangrove river at dusk, past the old coral mosque
d-kongo-dugout.story: Coral Spirit has worked Diani's northern river for ten years. At the end of the day its guides take you up the Mwachema through the mangroves, past the birdlife and an old cave passage, and back down to the mouth where the Kongo Mosque stands among the baobabs. The same flat water is used for stand-up paddleboarding, and a bonfire barbecue on the beach is the add-on. The web store shows every trip as sold out; in practice you book by phone or WhatsApp a day ahead. After rain the river runs murky, which is the season, not a fault.
d-kongo-dugout.why: Book it by phone, not online, and go in the last two hours of light on a rising tide.
facts: Daily, the last two hours of light, rising tide
Phone or WhatsApp +254 716 440 223, a day ahead
The bonfire barbecue on the beach after

k-kinondo.name: Kaya Kinondo
k-kinondo.teaser: The only sacred Mijikenda forest open to visitors: a black kaniki wrap, a Digo guide, no exceptions
k-kinondo.story: Kaya Kinondo is thirty hectares of coral-rag forest sacred to the Digo, a national monument since 1992 and part of the UNESCO Sacred Mijikenda Kaya Forests since 2008. In 2001 the elders offered a sacrifice to the ancestors and opened it to controlled visits, the first kaya ecotourism project in Kenya. You wrap a black kaniki cloth over your clothes, take off any hat, and walk with a Digo guide past the Chidzumba Cha Mwana Mlungu prayer hut, the medicinal trees and the 'hugging tree'. Afterwards an all-female Digo troupe dances to kayamba rhythms, if you have booked it.
k-kinondo.why: Treat it as a church visit, because it is one: stay on the path, take not even a leaf, ask before any photo.
facts: Daytime; departures around 10:00 and 15:00. Reserve via WhatsApp +254 745 797 653
Tours KES 1,000–2,000 reported, packages with transfer KES 6,000 (seen Oct 2025); agree before starting, M-Pesa or cash
Morning, or from 15:00; midday at the canopy edge is brutal
The Digo women's dance, booked ahead

k-system.name: The kaya system, honestly
k-system.teaser: More sacred forests line this very road, and none of them is an attraction
k-system.story: In 2008 UNESCO inscribed ten forest sites along some 200 km of this coast. They are the remains of fortified Mijikenda villages, founded from the sixteenth century, abandoned as villages by the 1940s and kept ever since as the dwelling places of ancestors. The National Museums have identified dozens more makaya beyond the inscribed ten, and guidebooks place some along the Diani road itself, near the golf course and Diani Sea Lodge. They are closed, and that is the point. Kaya Kinondo is the one door the elders have opened, on their own terms. Treat the rest as you would a locked church.
k-system.why: Visit the one that is open and leave the others alone: their closure is the tradition working.
facts: Kaya Kinondo, the one kaya open to visitors, with a Digo guide

k-colobus.name: Colobus Conservation & the colobridges
k-colobus.teaser: Rope ladders over the traffic, and the rescue centre that strung them after too many dead monkeys
k-colobus.story: Colobus Conservation was founded in 1997 because the road was killing Diani's monkeys. The Angolan black-and-white colobus, listed as Vulnerable, lives in the forest that a nine-kilometre road cut through in 1971, and cars still hit an average of 55 monkeys a year. The answer was the colobridges: rope ladders slung over Diani Beach Road, about thirty of them, densest toward the south. Look up long enough and a troop crosses hand over hand above the matatus. A 24-hour rescue line answers some 500 primates in distress a year, and the guided tour walks you past the rehabilitation enclosures.
k-colobus.why: Pay for the tour, then drive the beach road slowly for the rest of your stay: that is the whole lesson.
facts: Tour fee unpublished; cashless payment on arrival
A troop crossing a colobridge overhead

k-jadini.name: The Jadini forest patches
k-jadini.teaser: The strip's last coastal hardwood, named after a hotel and kept alive by its monkeys
k-jadini.story: The surviving patches of coastal hardwood toward the south end of the strip still carry the name of a hotel, Jadini, though the forest is more properly the Diani Forest. It is full of birds and butterflies, vervets and colobus, and it loses ground every year. You do not visit it so much as notice it: the canopy closing over the road, the rope bridges overhead, a troop on the power lines at first light. There is no gate, no ticket and no trail to follow. What it asks of you is small and permanent: drive this road slowly from now on.
k-jadini.why: Look up on the southern strip at dawn, when the troops are on the move above the road.
facts: Southern Diani Beach Road, around Colobus Conservation
Monkeys on the power lines at first light

k-turtle.name: Diani Turtle Watch
k-turtle.teaser: Fourteen monitors, fifty kilometres of coast, and now and then a hatchling release at dawn
k-turtle.story: Since 2012 Diani has had its own community turtle programme. Its monitors patrol the south coast every morning, move at-risk nests to accredited hatchery points on hotel beachfronts, answer strandings and run necropsies, which keep finding plastic. Hatchlings emerge 55 to 75 days after laying, and sponsored nests had produced more than 441 of them by January 2025. There is no ticket desk and no promise. Follow @dianiturtlewatch, tell your hotel's beach team you want the call, and listen for news of a release; when one comes it is at dawn or dusk, with a few hours' notice.
k-turtle.why: If a release is announced while you are here, drop everything else that day.

k-mikoko.name: Mikoko Pamoja, Gazi Bay
k-mikoko.teaser: The world's first community blue-carbon project, where mangrove credits pay for village wells
k-mikoko.story: Mikoko Pamoja means 'mangroves together', and since 2010 it has been the world's first community blue-carbon project. Gazi's villagers co-manage 117 hectares of mangroves, replant some 8,000 trees a year and sell credits for the carbon those trees lock away. The money has paid for clean water for 3,500 people and books for 700 children. The project is Plan Vivo-certified, won the UN Equator Prize in 2017, and has been copied down the coast and studied worldwide. Visits are arranged through the project itself; this is a working conservation office, not an attraction, so pay fairly for the guides' time.
k-mikoko.why: Arrange it ahead, walk the replanted plots with the team, and pay for their time.
facts: Gazi village, about 25 km south of Diani
Donation or guiding fee, agreed ahead
The replanted plots with the project team

c-kongo.name: Kongo Mosque
c-kongo.teaser: A coral mosque at the river mouth: its age is argued over, its use is not
c-kongo.story: At the Mwachema mouth, under the baobabs, stands the last relic of Diani's old Swahili settlements. Its age is argued: the heritage inventory says 14th–15th century, the press and local tradition say older. By the deputy imam's account the name comes from a grave inscription, 'Siddiq Kongo', found at the site; it was once called the Diani Persian Mosque. Tradition says it stood empty after the traders left until it was found again some three centuries ago. What nobody disputes is that it is alive: hundreds at Friday prayers, thousands spilling onto the beach at Eid, and a recent renovation that kept the ancient shell.
c-kongo.why: Dress properly on the sand beside it, ask before entering outside prayer times, and treat the graves as graves.
facts: A working mosque; ask before entering outside prayer times
The coral walls framed by the baobabs
Heritage inventory: 14th–15th century; press and tradition: 16th century or older

sources.label: Nation: Iconic Kongo mosque believed to be oldest in East Africa

c-shimoni-caves.name: The Shimoni caves & the shrine
c-shimoni-caves.teaser: The shackles are still in the coral, and one chamber is still a shrine: both histories are true
c-shimoni-caves.story: In the 18th and early 19th centuries these coral chambers held enslaved people waiting for the dhows to the markets of Zanzibar and Pemba. Iron shackles and chain studs are still fixed in the rock, according to National Museums of Kenya curators. Shimoni means 'the place of the hole', and the caves were sacred to Digo elders before that trade used them. One chamber is still a working shrine, with red, white and black cloths, rosewater and incense, and the guides explain the colours. Shrine, atrocity, shrine again: the south coast's memory sits in one room of coral.
c-shimoni-caves.why: Go with the community guide and let it be heavy; the fee pays Shimoni's teachers and dispensary medicine.
facts: Guided visits, two sessions a day reported (about 08:30–10:30 and 13:30–18:00, unverified)
The shrine chamber and what its colours mean

c-pillar-tomb.name: The Wasini pillar tomb
c-pillar-tomb.teaser: Chinese porcelain set into a Swahili tomb: the whole Indian Ocean trade in one object
c-pillar-tomb.story: Wasini's old Wa-vumba settlement is built in and around its own ruins, and among them stands a pillar tomb that still holds its inset Chinese porcelain. Read it slowly and it tells you what moved on the monsoon: goods from the far side of the ocean, the people who sailed with them, and the taste of a coast that wanted those goods set into its most solemn buildings. It sits thirty seconds off the village path, so it costs you nothing but a short detour during the island hour of the dhow day. Look closely, and leave every piece where it is.
c-pillar-tomb.why: Ask your boat crew to point it out: thirty seconds off the path, and it explains the coast.
facts: Wasini village, just off the main path
The island hour of the dhow day
The porcelain set into the pillar

l-baobab.name: The Galu baobab
l-baobab.teaser: The traditional southern end of Diani Beach is not a sign or a post but a tree
l-baobab.story: Diani's core runs from the Kongo river south to Galu, and the traditional southern marker is an old baobab: a boundary drawn in botany rather than surveying. Baobabs punctuate the whole strip. The bar at The 41 is built around one, and giants frame the mosque at the northern end. They are protected in practice by reverence, which on this coast is older than any law, and the sacred kaya forests nearby explain where that reverence comes from. Find the Galu tree on a beach walk and you have reached the end of Diani as the people who live here count it.
l-baobab.why: Walk south until you reach it: the tree, not the map, tells you where Diani ends.
facts: The baobab inside The 41's bar, on the way back

l-airstrip.name: Ukunda airstrip
l-airstrip.teaser: A short tarmac runway between beach and highway: the coast's side door from Nairobi
l-airstrip.story: The Kenya Airports Authority owns it, everyone calls it Diani Airport, and it is the coast's side door. Safarilink and Jambojet connect it with Nairobi daily, about an hour on Jambojet, which is why a Diani week no longer has to begin at the Likoni ferry. The runway sits between the beach and the highway; it was about 1.2 km long before the first phase of an upgrade added some 200 metres and a new apron. The skydivers' Caravans use it too, and their beach landings are briefed in the water section. Transfers and timings sit in the appendix.
l-airstrip.why: Fly in here from Nairobi and you skip Mombasa altogether.
facts: Safarilink or Jambojet from Nairobi, about an hour

l-two-fishes.name: The Two Fishes ruin
l-two-fishes.teaser: Once one of Diani's ten big hotels, now a lived-in ruin: the strip's reminder of how it ends
l-two-fishes.story: The Two Fishes was German-founded and, until the 1990s, one of the ten major hotels on Diani. It did not survive the contraction. Its shell is now lived in and worked around by local families, a condition the anthropologist Franziska Fay studied in a 2023 paper on 'the politics of skeletons and ruination'. It is not a sight to visit: people live there, and it is their home, not a photo stop. But knowing it is there recalibrates every brochure superlative on the strip, including the ones you will read about the hotels still standing either side of it.
l-two-fishes.why: See it from the road and keep going: it is a neighbourhood now, not a set.
facts: Southern strip, seen from the road
Franziska Fay, Journal of Eastern African Studies 17 (2023)

l-mteza.name: The Mteza bridge
l-mteza.teaser: Kenya's longest bridge over water, and the reason your transfer no longer waits for a ferry
l-mteza.story: The Mteza bridge is the centrepiece of the Dongo Kundu bypass: 1,440 metres long, the longest bridge over water in Kenya, opened to traffic in August 2024 and financed through Japan's aid agency, JICA. It ended the Likoni ferry's monopoly on the south coast, and with it the queue that used to define arriving in Diani. Most visitors cross it in the back of an airport transfer without noticing, which is exactly the point of it: the south coast now begins with a bridge instead of a wait. Whether you pay to cross is told in the arrival card.
l-mteza.why: Look out of the window as you cross: this is the bridge that turned Diani into an easy drive.
facts: On the Dongo Kundu bypass, the Mombasa approach
